amendments.rule: An inflected verb may align to an English subject pronoun, auxiliary, and main verb together. Choose the lexical English verb as the target head. **This permission is specific to a pronoun realizing the verb's person and number.** A lexical English subject noun the ASV supplies where no source nominal is present answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit: `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* gives *shall dwell* to the verb and leaves *men* `added`. **A presentative dummy *there* is not such a lexical subject.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb or participle with a presentative frame — `יֵּצֵא` → *there came forth*, `נִשֵּׂאת` → *there was lifted up* — the dummy belongs to the verb's unit, by the same constructional reasoning that puts it on `הָיָה` under rule 21, and the unit still heads on the lexical verb. When the verse also has an explicit subject noun, that noun's tokens are its own unit and only a genuinely pleonastic pronoun stays with the verb. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus an explicit subject pronoun as a relative clause, the English *who* or *which* realizes the pronoun; the waw is `unrepresented` if the ASV writes no separate connective.** Do not give the relative pronoun to the waw merely because it opens the recast clause: `וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו` → *which was behind him* gives *which* to `הוּא` and leaves the waw unrepresented, and `וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי` → *who am old* gives *who* to `אֲנִי` on the same terms. **A question auxiliary the ASV fronts belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb.** English marks a yes-or-no question by fronting an auxiliary, and where `הֲ` stands in the clause that word is what the ASV has written for it: `הֲלוֹא לֶאֱמוּנָה` → *do not thine eyes look upon truth* gives *do* to `הֲ` in a clause that has no verb at all to take it, and `הַעַל אֵלֶּה לֹא אֶפְקֹד` → *Shall I not visit* gives *Shall* to `הֲ` and *I visit* to the verb, even though that auxiliary also carries the imperfect's future. The `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question is read the same way, since it is what marks that clause as the second question: `אִם לֹא תָחִילוּ` → *will ye not tremble* gives *will* to `אִם` and *ye tremble* to the verb. Where the ASV marks the question by inversion alone and writes no auxiliary, the particle is `unrepresented`: `הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ` → *Fear ye not me*. Two limits. Where no interrogative morpheme is present at all, a fronted *do* is the verb's own under this rule's first sentence: `לֹא שָׁפָטוּ` → *do they not judge*. And this governs the yes-or-no particle only: an interrogative word that has an English word of its own — `מָה` → *what*, `אֵי` → *How* — leaves the fronted auxiliary to the verb, as `אֵי לָזֹאת אֶסְלַח לָךְ` → *How can I pardon thee* leaves *can I pardon* whole.
amendments.why: The contract says nothing about interrogative particles, and rule 17's opening permission — verb takes subject pronoun, auxiliary and main verb — is what otherwise pulls *Shall* and *will* onto the verb and leaves `הֲ` and the disjunctive `אִם` `unrepresented`. JER.5 settles it four times over and the anchor is JER.5.3, where the Hebrew clause is verbless and the *do* of *do not thine eyes look upon truth* can be nothing but the particle's rendering; JER.5.9, JER.5.22 and JER.5.29 fill the same fronted slot with *Shall* and *will*, and JER.5.28's *do they not judge*, which has no interrogative morpheme, is the control that keeps the auxiliary on the verb where no particle is present. The corpus agrees and does not contradict: it aligns a `Ti` to a fronted modal in four units across four chapters, all headed on that word — GEN.34.31 `הַ` → *should* and JDG.9.9 `הֶ` → *should*, each leaving the verb its own words. The wh-word limit is JER.5.7, JER.5.15 and JER.5.31, where `אֵי` and `מָה` already have *How* and *what* and the fronted *can* and *will* stay with the verb; without that limit the new clause would strip auxiliaries off verbs in every wh-question. Amending rule 17 rather than adding a rule keeps the qualification where the over-broad sentence stands.

conventions: Interrogative particles take the question auxiliary the ASV fronts for them, and the verb keeps its subject pronoun and lexical verb: הֲ → *do* (5.3, in a clause with no verb to take it), *Shall* (5.9, 5.29), and the אִם opening the following disjunctive question → *shall* (5.9, 5.29), *will* (5.22). Where the ASV marks the question by inversion alone and writes no auxiliary, the particle is `unrepresented`: הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ → *Fear ye not me* (5.22). Where no interrogative morpheme is present, the fronted *do* is the verb's own: לֹא שָׁפָטוּ → *do they not judge* (5.28). An interrogative that has an English word of its own — מָה → *what* (5.15, 5.31), אֵי → *How* (5.7) — leaves the auxiliary to the verb.

בְּגוֹי אֲשֶׁר כָּזֶה (5.9 and 5.29, which are the same verse but for 5.9's extra waw) splits the correlative: כְּ → *such* and אֲשֶׁר → *as*, each present morpheme taking a word the ASV wrote. The competing reading gives *such ... as* wholly to כְּ and leaves אֲשֶׁר `unrepresented`. Both verses are aligned the same way and must be changed together if ever changed.

עַל־כֵּן (5.6 *Wherefore*, 5.27 *therefore*) and לָכֵן (5.2 *surely*, 5.14 *Wherefore*) fuse under rule 30 and head on the first token, which is the one MACULA gives the compound lemma; heading on כֵּן is the competing reading. All four are headed the same way. Where the fused expression is instead an interrogative, the head is the wh-word: תַּחַת מֶה → *Wherefore* heads on מֶה (5.19), אֵי לָזֹאת → *How* on אֵי (5.7).

A contiguous interrogative expression the ASV renders by one English word fuses whole under rule 30 even where the English carries only the wh-word's sense and the rest goes unrendered: תַּחַת מֶה → *Wherefore* (5.19) and אֵי לָזֹאת → *How* (5.7) are each one unit, not one rendered morpheme beside `unrepresented` neighbours. Rule 30's disclaimer that such an expression need not be idiomatic is general rather than local to its אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה example, and rule 35's *carries every morpheme's sense* governs fusion across distance, not this — בְּיַד → *by* fuses a lexeme the English drops. 5.7 was reconciled to 5.19 on this ground.

report: Read all 65 candidate groups, then the dump end to end for the `added` units, which the lemma table cannot see. One real split found: the fusion of a fixed interrogative expression. JER.5.19 fuses תַּחַת מֶה into a single unit on *Wherefore* under rule 30, while JER.5.7 split the parallel אֵי לָזֹאת, giving *How* to אֵי and marking לָ and זֹאת `unrepresented`. Nothing in the source licenses the difference: both are contiguous interrogative expressions the ASV renders by one English word, and rule 30 names the split shape expressly as what not to do ('the whole expression is one unit ... rather than one rendered morpheme beside others marked unrepresented'). JER.5.7 is patched to the fused reading; JER.5.19 stands.

The verse note's ground for splitting — 'that expression is not a fixed lexical idiom' — is disclaimed by rule 30's own text ('Do not read fixed multi-word Hebrew expression above as a requirement that the pair be idiomatic'), and rule 35's 'carries every morpheme's sense' governs fusion across distance rather than this: בְּיַד → *by* and מִפְּנֵי → *because of* fuse lexemes the English drops. The chapter's other rule-30 fusions all go the same way — לָכֵן (5.2, 5.14), עַל־כֵּן (5.6, 5.27), מֵהֵנָּה → *thence* (5.6), מֵעוֹלָם → *ancient* (5.15), אֲשֶׁר בָּ → *wherein* (5.17) — and 5.7 was the lone outlier, the only place in the chapter where a demonstrative went unrendered.

Everything else the table flagged is context doing its work. The near-identical twins JER.5.9 and JER.5.29 agree unit for unit, including the contested כְּ → *such* / אֲשֶׁר → *as* split and the extra waw only 5.9 has. עַל־כֵּן and לָכֵן all four head on the first token. The article-plus-demonstrative phrases (5.14, 5.18, 5.23, 5.25) uniformly leave both article morphemes `unrepresented` and give the determiner to the demonstrative that licenses it, per rule 41's 'only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner'. אֵת takes English only at 5.5 (*speak unto*, rule 16's first family) and is `unrepresented` at 5.3, 5.7, 5.14, 5.19, 5.22, 5.24, where the ASV writes the object bare.

The nine `added` units are consistent with each other and with rules 42, 51 and 55: supplied connectives in asyndetic clauses (5.3 *but*, 5.4 *nor*, 5.5 *and* twice, 5.6 *and*), supplied subordinators for finite clauses with no relative morpheme (5.17 *which*, 5.24 *that*, 5.22 *though* beside a waw that already has its *and*), and the supplied lexical verb *look* at 5.3, where לְ has already spent its own *upon* (rule 20's lexical-verb boundary). No verse folds such a word into a neighbouring unit, so the chapter is internally uniform on this. 5.24's two *that*s differ only because the first has an article morpheme and the second does not — rule 46's closing sentence, not a split.

BSB disagreements: no genuine error among them except the two now patched. JER.5.7 זֹאת and one of the 5.7 R-class tokens were the real ones and are corrected. The remaining R × 6, the Td × 7, 5.2 לַ, 5.23 לָ and 5.31 בַ are the documented convention difference — ASV recastings under rules 21, 27, 40 and articles under rules 29 and 41 — where BSB attaches the morpheme to its phrase; 5.7 and 5.19 אוֹתִ/אוֹתָ are rule 16 before a bare object; 5.7 וַ is the surplus-waw count (two waws, one written *and*, given to the waw opening the clause the *and* opens); 5.17 הֵנָּה is the resumptive after *wherein*, rule 22. None of these is changed, and none should be changed to raise the rate.

Recorded four conventions: the interrogative-particle judgment, the 5.9/5.29 correlative split, the fusion-head choice for עַל־כֵּן and לָכֵן, and the outcome of the 5.7 reconciliation. One amendment returned, to rule 17, on the fronted question auxiliary; no new rules, since rule 30 already decides the fusion case and only needed applying.
